questions.explanation: Uniqueness needs the field, and both of its parts, to tend to $\mathbf 0$ at infinity. A constant field never does. Its divergence and curl are both 0, so the other "reasons" are false, and $\mathbb R^3$ is simply connected.

questions.stem:
A smooth field $\mathbf F$ is zero outside some ball, and $
abla\cdot\mathbf F = 0$ everywhere. What does the Helmholtz decomposition $\mathbf F = -
abla\phi + 
abla	imes\mathbf A$ give?
questions.explanation: $\phi = \dfrac{1}{4\pi}\displaystyle\iiint\frac{\nabla\cdot\mathbf F}{|\mathbf x - \mathbf y|}\,dV$, and the integrand is 0, so $\phi = 0$. The divergence of $\mathbf F$ is the source of $\phi$, and the curl of $\mathbf F$ is the source of $\mathbf A$. (A nonzero constant $\phi$ would also give $\nabla\phi = \mathbf 0$, but the formula gives exactly 0.)

questions.stem: Which statements about the magnetic vector potential are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Because $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B = 0$ on all of space, $\mathbf B = \nabla\times\mathbf A$ for some $\mathbf A$
Replacing $\mathbf A$ by $\mathbf A + \nabla\chi$ changes $\mathbf B$
The Coulomb gauge is the condition $\nabla\cdot\mathbf A = 0$
In magnetostatics in the Coulomb gauge, $\nabla^2\mathbf A = -\mu_0\mathbf J$
questions.explanation:
All of space is star-shaped, so a solenoidal $\mathbf B$ is a curl. $
abla	imes(\mathbf A + 
abla\chi) = 
abla	imes\mathbf A$, so a gauge transformation leaves $\mathbf B$ alone. Ampère's law $
abla	imes\mathbf B = \mu_0\mathbf J$ becomes $
abla(
abla\cdot\mathbf A) - 
abla^2\mathbf A = \mu_0\mathbf J$, and with $
abla\cdot\mathbf A = 0$ this is $
abla^2\mathbf A = -\mu_0\mathbf J$.

questions.stem: The picture shows two regions of space with a hole. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Two shaded boxes standing for regions of space. Left: a vertical dashed line with a loop around it. Right: a small hollow dot inside a sphere. Numbered markers sit on the line, the loop, the dot and the sphere.

questions.explanation: Left: space minus a line. A loop around the line cannot shrink to a point, so a curl-free field there (the vortex field) can fail to be a gradient. Right: space minus a point. A sphere around the point cannot shrink to a point, so a divergence-free field there ($\mathbf x/|\mathbf x|^3$) can fail to be a curl.

questions.stem: With $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$, what is $\nabla\times\langle 0,\; 0,\; -\ln r\rangle$ (away from the $z$-axis)?
questions.explanation: For $\mathbf A = \langle 0, 0, h\rangle$, $\nabla\times\mathbf A = \langle h_y, -h_x, 0\rangle$. With $h = -\ln r$, $h_x = -x/r^2$ and $h_y = -y/r^2$, so the curl is $\langle -y, x, 0\rangle/r^2$: the vortex field. The first choice has the opposite sign, the second is $-\nabla h$ (a gradient, not a curl), and the third has the wrong power of $r$.

questions.stem: Helmholtz published his paper on vortex motion, which gave the decomposition its name, in the year ___.
questions.explanation: Hermann von Helmholtz's paper on vortex motion appeared in 1858 in Crelle's journal. George Stokes had used the same decomposition earlier, in an 1849 paper on diffraction.

cards.back: $\iint_S\mathbf g\cdot d\mathbf S = -4\pi GM_{\text{enc}}$; differential form $\nabla\cdot\mathbf g = -4\pi G\rho$.

cards.front: Field of a spherically symmetric body at radius $r$
cards.back: $g(r) = -GM_{\text{enc}}(r)/r^2$ (radial, inward): only the mass closer to the center counts.
Outside a spherically symmetric body: same field as a point mass at the center. Inside a uniform hollow shell: zero field.
$|\mathbf g| = GMr/R^3 = g_0\,r/R$: linear in $r$, zero at the center, largest at the surface.
Simple harmonic motion $x'' = -(g_0/R)x$, period $2\pi\sqrt{R/g_0}$ (about 84 min for Earth), same as a surface-skimming orbit.

cards.front: Potential of a thin uniform shell
cards.back: $\Phi = -GM/r$ outside, constant $-GM/R$ inside (so $\mathbf g = \mathbf 0$ inside).

$
abla^2\Phi = 4\pi Gho$ (from $
abla\cdot\mathbf g = -4\pi Gho$ and $\mathbf g = -
abla\Phi$); $
abla^2\Phi = 0$ in empty space.

cards.front: Field of an infinite sheet of mass
cards.back: $|\mathbf g| = 2\pi G\sigma$ toward the sheet, the same at every distance (pillbox argument).

cards.front: When does Gauss's law find the field?
cards.back: Only with symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, planar) that makes $\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf n$ constant or zero on a surface. Otherwise it is true but gives only the total flux.

cards.front: Why Maxwell added the displacement current
cards.back: $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}\mathbf B = 0$ would force $\nabla\cdot\mathbf J = 0$; adding $\mu_0\varepsilon_0\,\partial\mathbf E/\partial t$ restores charge conservation.

$
abla	imes(
abla	imes\mathbf F) = 
abla(
abla\cdot\mathbf F) - 
abla^2\mathbf F$ (vector Laplacian componentwise).

cards.front: Wave equation for $\mathbf E$ in vacuum
cards.back: $\nabla^2\mathbf E = \mu_0\varepsilon_0\,\partial^2\mathbf E/\partial t^2$, speed $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} \approx 2.998\times10^8$ m/s.
$\mathbf E = E_0\cos(kz - \omega t)\mathbf i$, $\mathbf B = (E_0/c)\cos(kz - \omega t)\mathbf j$, $\omega = ck$: in phase, perpendicular, transverse.
$\nabla\cdot\mathbf E = 0$ forces $\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf E_0 = 0$; then $\mathbf B = \frac1\omega\mathbf k\times\mathbf E$.
$u = \frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|\mathbf E|^2 + \frac{1}{2\mu_0}|\mathbf B|^2$; in a plane wave the two parts are equal.
$\mathbf S = \frac1{\mu_0}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$; $\partial u/\partial t + \nabla\cdot\mathbf S = -\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$.
$I = \frac{E_0B_0}{2\mu_0} = \frac12c\varepsilon_0E_0^2$ (the average of $\cos^2$ is $\frac12$).

$
abla\cdot(\mathbf E	imes\mathbf B) = \mathbf B\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf E) - \mathbf E\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf B)$.

cards.front: Flux of the gradient of a harmonic function
cards.back: $\iint_S\partial u/\partial n\,dS = \iiint\nabla^2u\,dV = 0$ through every closed surface.

cards.front: Proof idea of the mean value property
cards.back: The sphere average $A(r)$ has $A'(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi r^2}\iint\partial u/\partial n\,dS = 0$, so $A(r) = \lim_{r\to0}A = u(\mathbf p)$.

No stable electrostatic equilibrium for a point charge in a charge-free region: $V$ is harmonic, so $qV$ has no strict local minimum.

cards.front: Second-derivative test on a harmonic $f(x, y)$
cards.back: $f_{xx} = -f_{yy}$, so $D = -f_{xx}^2 - f_{xy}^2 \le 0$: never a strict local max or min.
Irrotational + incompressible: $\mathbf v = \nabla\phi$, $\nabla^2\phi = 0$, and $\partial\phi/\partial n = 0$ on solid walls.

$K = \kappa_1\kappa_2$ and $H = (\kappa_1 + \kappa_2)/2$, from the principal curvatures.

cards.front: Principal curvatures at a horizontal tangent plane
cards.back: Eigenvalues of the Hessian $\mathcal H$ of $z = f(x, y)$; normal curvature is $\mathbf u^T\mathcal H\mathbf u$ and $K = \det\mathcal H$.
$\kappa(\theta) = \kappa_1\cos^2\theta + \kappa_2\sin^2\theta$, with $\theta$ measured from the first principal direction.

$\iint_S K\,dA = 2\pi\chi(S)$, $\chi = V - E + F = 2 - 2g$: $4\pi$ for a sphere, 0 for a torus.
$K = \dfrac{\cos v}{b(a + b\cos v)}$: $+4\pi$ total on the outer half, $-4\pi$ on the inner half.

cards.front: Cyclic property of the scalar triple product
cards.back: $\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) = \mathbf b\cdot(\mathbf c\times\mathbf a) = \mathbf c\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)$; swapping two vectors flips the sign

cards.front: Distance from $Q$ to the line $P + t\mathbf v$

cards.front: Closest point of the line $P + t\mathbf v$ to $Q$

cards.front: Closest points of two skew lines
cards.back: Solve $\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf v_1 = 0$ and $\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf v_2 = 0$ for $t, s$, where $\mathbf w = \mathbf r_1(t) - \mathbf r_2(s)$

cards.front: Two non-parallel lines with $\overrightarrow{P_1P_2}\cdot(\mathbf v_1\times\mathbf v_2) = 0$
cards.back: They intersect (they lie in one plane)

cards.front: Eigenvalues of $\begin{bmatrix} A & h\\ h & C\end{bmatrix}$
cards.back: $\lambda = \dfrac{A + C}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{A - C}{2}\right)^2 + h^2}$

cards.front: Quadric $Q(x, y, z) = 1$ from eigenvalue signs
cards.back: No negatives: ellipsoid; one: hyperboloid of one sheet; two: two sheets; three: no points; a zero: degenerate

cards.front: Quadratic forms and the second-derivative test
cards.back: $D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2 > 0$: ellipse-like (extremum); $D < 0$: hyperbola-like (saddle)
$\dfrac{d\mathbf T}{ds} = \kappa\mathbf N$, $\dfrac{d\mathbf N}{ds} = -\kappa\mathbf T + \tau\mathbf B$, $\dfrac{d\mathbf B}{ds} = -\tau\mathbf N$

cards.front: Why $d\mathbf B/ds$ is parallel to $\mathbf N$
cards.back: It is perpendicular to $\mathbf B$ (constant length) and to $\mathbf T$ (differentiate $\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf T = 0$), leaving only $\mathbf N$.

cards.front: Curvature and torsion of $\langle a\cos t,\, a\sin t,\, bt\rangle$

cards.front: Torsion of the twisted cubic $\langle t, t^2, t^3\rangle$

cards.back: The curve lies in a plane ($\mathbf B$ is constant).

1. Ellipse with the Sun at a focus. 2. Equal areas in equal times. 3. $T^2 \propto a^3$.

cards.front: Why central forces conserve $\mathbf h = \mathbf r\times\mathbf v$
cards.back: $\mathbf h' = \mathbf v\times\mathbf v + \mathbf r\times\mathbf a = \mathbf 0$ because $\mathbf a\parallel\mathbf r$.

$r = \dfrac{h^2/GM}{1 + e\cos\theta}$, a conic with the center of force at a focus

cards.front: Kepler's third law with the constant
cards.back: $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}a^3$; around the Sun in years and AU, $T^2 = a^3$

cards.front: What differentiability at a point guarantees
cards.back: Continuity there, both partials, and $D_{\mathbf u}f = \nabla f\cdot\mathbf u$ for every unit $\mathbf u$.

cards.front: Continuous, all directional derivatives, not differentiable
cards.back: $\dfrac{x^2y}{x^2 + y^2}$: $D_{\mathbf u}f(0,0) = u_1^2u_2$, not $\nabla f\cdot\mathbf u = 0$.

cards.front: All directional derivatives exist, yet not continuous
cards.back: $\dfrac{xy^2}{x^2 + y^4}$: slopes $u_2^2/u_1$ along lines, but $f = \tfrac12$ on $x = y^2$.

cards.front: Idea of the proof of Clairaut's theorem
cards.back: The second difference $\Delta$ equals $h^2f_{xy}(p) = h^2f_{yx}(q)$ (mean value theorem twice, in each order); let $h \to 0$ using continuity.

cards.front: Derivative matrix of $\mathbf F: \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^m$
cards.back: $m\times n$ matrix of $\partial F_i/\partial x_j$. Row $i$ = $\nabla F_i$; column $j$ = $\partial\mathbf F/\partial x_j$.
$\mathbf F(\mathbf a + \mathbf h) \approx \mathbf F(\mathbf a) + D\mathbf F(\mathbf a)\,\mathbf h$
$D(\mathbf G\circ\mathbf F)(\mathbf a) = D\mathbf G(\mathbf F(\mathbf a))\,D\mathbf F(\mathbf a)$: outer (at $\mathbf F(\mathbf a)$) times inner.

cards.front: Derivative matrix of the polar map
cards.back: $D\mathbf P = \begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta & -r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}$, $\det D\mathbf P = r$
$f_x = z_r\cos\theta - \dfrac{z_\theta\sin\theta}{r}$, $f_y = z_r\sin\theta + \dfrac{z_\theta\cos\theta}{r}$, $|\nabla f|^2 = z_r^2 + \dfrac{z_\theta^2}{r^2}$

cards.front: Why the inverse is only local (polar map)
cards.back: $\det = r \ne 0$ for $r > 0$, but $\theta$ and $\theta + 2\pi$ give the same point, so $\mathbf P$ is not one-to-one overall.

cards.back: $u = e^{-\alpha n^2t}\sin nx$ solves $u_t = \alpha u_{xx}$: higher frequencies decay faster.

cards.front: Mean value property and maximum principle
cards.back: A harmonic function equals its average on circles; if not constant, it has no interior max or min.

cards.back: Area of $D \approx A(B)\times\dfrac{\text{points in } D}{N}$

abla^2Rangle$ in Cartesian coordinates. It appears in $
abla	imes(
abla	imes\mathbf F) = 
abla(
abla\cdot\mathbf F) - 
abla^2\mathbf F$.
A wave whose fields are the same over every plane perpendicular to its direction of travel, such as $\mathbf E = \mathbf E_0\cos(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x - \omega t)$.
Of a wave: oscillating at right angles to the direction of travel. Electromagnetic waves in vacuum are transverse because $\nabla\cdot\mathbf E = \nabla\cdot\mathbf B = 0$.
Energy conservation for electromagnetic fields: $\partial u/\partial t + \nabla\cdot\mathbf S = -\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$, with $u$ the field energy density and $\mathbf S$ the Poynting vector.
The energy flux of an electromagnetic field, $\mathbf S = \frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ (watts per square meter); for a wave it points along the direction of travel.
Of a wave: the time-averaged power carried per unit area; for an electromagnetic plane wave $I = \tfrac12c\varepsilon_0E_0^2$.
A harmonic function on a bounded connected region, continuous up to the boundary, takes its maximum and minimum on the boundary; if it takes either at an interior point, it is constant.

No arrangement of fixed charges can hold a point charge in stable equilibrium by electrostatic forces alone, because the potential in a charge-free region is harmonic and has no strict local minimum (Earnshaw, 1842).
A function $\phi$ with $\mathbf v = \nabla\phi$ for an irrotational flow (one with no net circulation around obstacles).
A model of an ideal fluid flow that is irrotational and incompressible, so $\mathbf v = \nabla\phi$ with $\nabla^2\phi = 0$ and $\partial\phi/\partial n = 0$ on solid walls. It ignores viscosity.
A point in a flow where the velocity is zero, such as the front and back of a cylinder in potential flow.
Potential flow predicts zero drag on an obstacle such as a cylinder, while real fluids exert drag; the gap comes from viscosity, which makes real flows separate and form a wake (d'Alembert, 1752).

At a point of a surface, $K = \kappa_1\kappa_2$, the product of the principal curvatures. For a graph $z = f(x, y)$, $K = (f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2)/(1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2)^2$; a sphere of radius $R$ has $K = 1/R^2$.
The signed curvature of the curve cut from a surface by the plane containing the normal $\mathbf n$ and a tangent direction $\mathbf u$; positive if it bends toward $\mathbf n$.

The largest and smallest normal curvatures $\kappa_1$, $\kappa_2$ at a point; they occur in perpendicular principal directions. Where the tangent plane is horizontal, they are the eigenvalues of the Hessian.
The average of the principal curvatures, $H = (\kappa_1 + \kappa_2)/2$. Unlike Gaussian curvature it is not intrinsic: rolling a flat sheet into a cylinder changes it.
In differential geometry: the normal curvature at angle $\theta$ from the first principal direction is $\kappa_1\cos^2\theta + \kappa_2\sin^2\theta$.
A point of a surface with $K > 0$: both principal curvatures have the same sign and the surface is dome-like there.
A point of a surface with $K < 0$: the principal curvatures have opposite signs and the surface is saddle-like there.
A point of a surface where both principal curvatures are 0. A point where exactly one is 0 (as on a cylinder) is called parabolic.
Gauss's "remarkable theorem" (1827): Gaussian curvature can be computed from distances and angles measured within the surface, so bending without stretching never changes it.
A curve on a surface that is as straight as the surface allows, locally the shortest path between its points; on a sphere, an arc of a great circle.
A triangle on a surface whose sides are geodesics; its angles satisfy $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = \pi + \iint_T K\,dA$.
$\chi = V - E + F$ for any subdivision of a closed surface into polygons; it depends only on topology: 2 for a sphere, 0 for a torus, $2 - 2g$ for a surface with $g$ holes.
For a closed surface, $\iint_S K\,dA = 2\pi\chi(S)$; for a geodesic triangle, the angle sum exceeds $\pi$ by $\iint_T K\,dA$.
$|\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b| \le |\mathbf a||\mathbf b|$ for any vectors, with equality exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other. It guarantees $|\cos\theta| \le 1$ in any dimension.
$|\mathbf u + \mathbf v| \le |\mathbf u| + |\mathbf v|$: one side of a triangle is never longer than the other two together. Equality holds when the vectors point the same way.
The vector $\mathbf a\times(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) = \mathbf b(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c) - \mathbf c(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b)$, which lies in the plane of $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$.
The point of a line (or plane) closest to a given point; for the line $P + t\mathbf v$ and point $Q$ it is at $t = \overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\mathbf v/(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v)$.
The shortest segment joining two skew lines. It meets both lines at right angles, points along $\mathbf v_1\times\mathbf v_2$, and its length is the distance between the lines.
A second-degree term with two different variables, such as $xy$, $yz$ or $xz$. Cross terms tilt a conic or quadric away from the coordinate axes.
A polynomial whose terms all have degree exactly 2, such as $Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2$; it can be written $\mathbf x^{T}M\mathbf x$ with a symmetric matrix $M$.
A square matrix equal to its transpose ($m_{ij} = m_{ji}$). The matrix of $Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2$ is symmetric, with diagonal $A, C$ and both off-diagonal entries $B/2$.
New coordinates on axes turned by an angle $\theta$: $x = x'\cos\theta - y'\sin\theta$, $y = x'\sin\theta + y'\cos\theta$. Choosing $\cot2\theta = (A - C)/B$ removes the $xy$ term.
A number $\lambda$ with $M\mathbf u = \lambda\mathbf u$ for some nonzero vector $\mathbf u$; for a $2\times2$ matrix, a root of $\det(M - \lambda I) = 0$.
A nonzero vector $\mathbf u$ that a matrix only stretches: $M\mathbf u = \lambda\mathbf u$. Any nonzero multiple of an eigenvector is also one.

A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and perpendicular unit eigenvectors; in coordinates along them a quadratic form becomes $\lambda_1x'^2 + \lambda_2y'^2 (+\,\lambda_3z'^2)$. (A linear algebra result, stated without proof in this course.)
The perpendicular eigenvector directions of a quadratic form, along which a tilted conic or quadric lines up with its standard form.
The derivatives of the TNB frame with respect to arc length: $\mathbf T' = \kappa\mathbf N$, $\mathbf N' = -\kappa\mathbf T + \tau\mathbf B$, $\mathbf B' = -\tau\mathbf N$.

The vector $\boldsymbol\omega = \tau\mathbf T + \kappa\mathbf B$; each frame vector satisfies $\mathbf X' = \boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf X$, so the TNB frame turns at the rate $\sqrt{\kappa^2 + \tau^2}$ per unit length.
Of a curve's property: determined by the curve's own shape, so unchanged by moving or rotating it. Curvature and torsion are intrinsic.
Given continuous $\kappa(s) > 0$ and $\tau(s)$, there is a curve parametrized by arc length with that curvature and torsion, unique up to a rotation and translation.
A stretch of road or track whose curvature changes gradually from 0 (straight) to $1/R$ (a circular arc), so that sideways acceleration builds up smoothly.
The plane curve whose curvature is proportional to arc length, $\kappa = s/A^2$; its coordinates are Fresnel integrals. Used as a transition curve on railways and highways.
The rate of change of acceleration with time, in m/s³. Along a clothoid at constant speed the lateral jerk is constant, $v^3/(RL)$.

Planets move on ellipses with the Sun at a focus; the Sun–planet line sweeps equal areas in equal times; $T^2$ is proportional to $a^3$. Newton derived all three from an inverse-square law of gravitation.
Each planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus; in polar form $r = \dfrac{h^2/GM}{1 + e\cos\theta}$.
The line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times: $dA/dt = h/2$ is constant. It holds for any central force.
The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis: $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}a^3$ (in years and AU around the Sun, $T^2 = a^3$).
A force that always points along the line through a fixed center, so the acceleration is parallel to $\mathbf r$. It keeps $\mathbf h = \mathbf r\times\mathbf v$ constant.
The point of an orbit around the Sun closest to the Sun, at distance $r_p = a(1 - e)$; the planet moves fastest there.
The point of an orbit around the Sun farthest from the Sun, at distance $r_a = a(1 + e)$; the planet moves slowest there.
A circle, ellipse, parabola or hyperbola. With a focus at the origin, $r = \dfrac{p}{1 + e\cos\theta}$.
The number $e$ in $r = p/(1 + e\cos\theta)$ that sets a conic's shape: $e = 0$ circle, $0 < e < 1$ ellipse, $e = 1$ parabola, $e > 1$ hyperbola.
Half the longest diameter of an ellipse, $a$; for an orbit, the average of the perihelion and aphelion distances.
A unit of length of exactly 149,597,870,700 m, about Earth's average distance from the Sun. In years and AU, Kepler's third law for the Sun is $T^2 = a^3$.
A specific example showing that a general statement is false, such as $\dfrac{xy}{x^2 + y^2}$, which has both partial derivatives at the origin but is not continuous there.

In the definition of differentiability, $E(h, k) = f(a + h, b + k) - f(a, b) - f_x(a,b)h - f_y(a,b)k$, the gap between the function and its tangent plane. $f$ is differentiable when $E/\sqrt{h^2 + k^2} \to 0$.
Having first partial derivatives that exist and are continuous (on an open set); also called a $C^1$ function. Such a function is differentiable.
If $g$ is continuous on $[p, q]$ and differentiable inside it, then $g(q) - g(p) = g'(c)(q - p)$ for some $c$ between $p$ and $q$.
The quantity $f(a + h, b + h) - f(a + h, b) - f(a, b + h) + f(a, b)$, which is about $h^2 f_{xy}(a, b)$ for small $h$; used to prove Clairaut's theorem.

For $\mathbf F: \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^m$, the $m\times n$ matrix $D\mathbf F$ of first partials $\partial F_i/\partial x_j$. Row $i$ is $\nabla F_i$; $\mathbf F(\mathbf a + \mathbf h) \approx \mathbf F(\mathbf a) + D\mathbf F(\mathbf a)\mathbf h$.
$D(\mathbf G\circ\mathbf F)(\mathbf a) = D\mathbf G(\mathbf F(\mathbf a))\,D\mathbf F(\mathbf a)$: the derivative of a composite is the product of the derivative matrices, outer times inner.
If $\mathbf F$ is $C^1$ and $\det D\mathbf F(\mathbf a) \ne 0$, then near $\mathbf a$ the map has a $C^1$ local inverse, whose derivative at $\mathbf F(\mathbf a)$ is $D\mathbf F(\mathbf a)^{-1}$.
A map that undoes $\mathbf F$ on a small neighborhood of a point, though perhaps not everywhere (the polar map has local inverses but is not one-to-one overall).
The PDE $u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}$ for vibrations and waves traveling at speed $c$; its solutions are $u = F(x - ct) + G(x + ct)$.
The PDE $u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0$ (or $\nabla^2u = 0$ in three variables); its solutions are the harmonic functions. It describes steady temperatures and electrostatic potentials.
For a linear homogeneous equation, any combination $c_1u_1 + c_2u_2$ of solutions is again a solution.
A solution of the form $F(x - ct)$ (moving right at speed $c$) or $F(x + ct)$ (moving left): a fixed shape that moves without changing.
The variables $\xi = x - ct$, $\eta = x + ct$ for the wave equation; in them it becomes $U_{\xi\eta} = 0$. The lines $x - ct = k$ and $x + ct = k$ ($k$ constant) are the characteristics.
The solution of $u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}$ with $u(x,0) = \varphi(x)$, $u_t(x,0) = \psi(x)$: $u = \tfrac12[\varphi(x - ct) + \varphi(x + ct)] + \tfrac{1}{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}\psi(s)\,ds$.
A harmonic function's value at the center of any circle (in two variables) or sphere (in three), whose disk or ball lies in its domain, equals its average value on that circle or sphere.
A quadratic form (or symmetric matrix) that is positive for every nonzero input. A positive definite Hessian at a critical point means a local minimum.
A quadratic form (or symmetric matrix) that is negative for every nonzero input. A negative definite Hessian at a critical point means a local maximum.
A quadratic form that takes both positive and negative values (its matrix has eigenvalues of both signs). An indefinite Hessian at a critical point means a saddle point.
The determinants $D_1, D_2, D_3, \dots$ of the top-left $1\times1$, $2\times2$, $3\times3$, … corners of a square matrix.
A symmetric matrix is positive definite exactly when all its leading principal minors are positive (and negative definite when their signs alternate $-, +, -, \dots$).
The Lagrange multiplier $\lambda$ read as the rate $dF/dk$ at which the optimal value changes when the constraint level $k$ changes: the value of one more unit of the limited resource.
The set of points that satisfy all the constraints of an optimization problem, such as $g(x, y) \le k$.
An inequality constraint $g \le k$ that holds with equality ($g = k$) at the optimum; the optimum lies on the edge of the feasible region.
An inequality constraint that holds strictly ($g < k$) at the optimum; it does not affect the answer, and its multiplier is 0.
Conditions for a maximum of $f$ subject to $g \le k$: $\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g$, $\lambda \ge 0$, $g \le k$ and $\lambda(g - k) = 0$. Named for Karush (1939) and Kuhn and Tucker (1951).
The KKT condition $\lambda(g - k) = 0$: either the multiplier is zero or the constraint is active.
Methods that start from a guess and improve it step by step, stopping when the steps stop mattering.
The iteration $\mathbf x_{n+1} = \mathbf x_n - \alpha\nabla f(\mathbf x_n)$, which steps in the direction of steepest decrease to search for a minimum.
The positive number $\alpha$ that scales the gradient in each gradient descent step; too large and the iterates diverge, too small and they crawl.
One of the successive approximations $\mathbf x_0, \mathbf x_1, \mathbf x_2, \dots$ produced by an iterative method.
Convergence in which each error is roughly a constant times the square of the previous one, so the number of correct digits about doubles each step (typical of Newton's method).
The rule that ends an iteration, such as stopping when $|\nabla f|$ falls below a small tolerance or after a maximum number of steps.

An approximation of $\iint_R f\,dA$: cut $R$ into sub-rectangles of area $\Delta A$ and add $f(\text{center})\,\Delta A$ over all of them. Its error is about $\frac{h^2}{24}\iint f_{xx}\,dA + \frac{k^2}{24}\iint f_{yy}\,dA$, so it has order of accuracy 2.

An approximation that fits parabolas through equally spaced values. On one interval: $\frac h3\big(f_0 + 4f_1 + f_2\big)$. In two variables the weights are products of $1, 4, 1$ (corners 1, edge midpoints 4, center 16, times $\frac{hk}{9}$). It is exact for polynomials of degree at most 3 in each variable, and its error is about proportional to $h^4$.

The power $p$ for which a numerical method's error is roughly proportional to $h^p$, where $h$ is the step size. The midpoint rule has order 2 (halving $h$ divides the error by about 4); Simpson's rule has order 4.

Estimating an integral from random samples: with $N$ uniform random points in a box $B$ containing $D$, $\iint_D f\,dA \approx A(B)\cdot\frac1N\sum g(P_i)$, where $g = f$ on $D$ and $0$ elsewhere. The error shrinks like $1/\sqrt N$ in any number of dimensions.

The standard deviation of an estimate that comes from random sampling. For a Monte Carlo integral it is about $A(B)\,s/\sqrt N$, where $s$ is the standard deviation of the sampled values; the estimate is within two standard errors of the true value roughly 95% of the time.

The rapid growth in work for grid methods as the number of variables grows: a grid with $n$ points per direction in $d$ dimensions needs $n^d$ points. It is the main reason Monte Carlo methods are used for integrals in many variables.

A double integral over an unbounded region, or of a function that is unbounded on the region. It is defined as a limit of integrals over bounded regions that avoid the trouble (an exhaustion), and it converges if that limit is finite.

A sequence of bounded regions $D_1 \subseteq D_2 \subseteq \cdots$, on each of which the integrand is continuous and bounded, that together fill up a region $D$. For $f \ge 0$, every exhaustion gives the same value of $\lim\iint_{D_n}f\,dA$.

Said of a function $f$ on a region $D$ when $\iint_D|f|\,dA$ is finite. For a function that changes sign, this is what makes an improper double integral well defined, and it is the hypothesis of the general Fubini theorem.

If $0 \le f \le g$ on $D$ and $\iint_D g\,dA$ converges, then $\iint_D f\,dA$ converges; if $\iint_D f\,dA$ diverges, so does $\iint_D g\,dA$. Powers $r^{-q}$ of the distance are the usual functions to compare with.

For a nonnegative integrand, the double integral and both iterated integrals are equal, whether finite or infinite; so nonnegative improper integrals may be iterated in either order. Published by Leonida Tonelli in 1909.
$I = I_{\text{cm}} + md^2$: the moment of inertia about any axis equals that about the parallel axis through the center of mass plus the mass times the squared distance between the axes.
$k = \sqrt{I/m}$: the distance from the axis at which all the mass, placed in a thin ring, would give the same moment of inertia.
Rolling in which the contact point is momentarily at rest, so the center moves at speed $v = \omega R$.
The ratio $C/(MR^2)$ of a planet's moment of inertia about its spin axis to $MR^2$; 0.4 for a uniform ball, smaller when mass is concentrated toward the center (about 0.331 for Earth).

A doughnut shape: strictly the surface swept out by revolving a circle of radius $a$ about an axis in its plane at distance $R > a$ from its center. Revolving the disk instead gives the solid torus, with volume $2\pi^2Ra^2$.
Coordinates $(s, \alpha, \theta)$ for a torus: $r = R + s\cos\alpha$, $z = s\sin\alpha$, with cylindrical $\theta$; $dV = s(R + s\cos\alpha)\,ds\,d\alpha\,d\theta$. (Other systems share the name.)
Revolving a plane region $D$ about an axis in its plane that does not cross it sweeps out volume $2\pi\bar rA$, where $A$ is the area of $D$ and $\bar r$ the distance of its centroid from the axis.
The set of points with $x_1^2 + \dots + x_n^2 \le a^2$ in $\mathbb R^n$; its volume is $V_n(1)a^n$ with $V_n(1) = \tfrac{2\pi}{n}V_{n-2}(1)$.
The plane with one point (usually the origin) removed. It is connected but not simply connected.

The field $\mathbf V = \left\langle\frac{-y}{x^2 + y^2}, \frac{x}{x^2 + y^2}\right\rangle$ on the punctured plane. It is locally the gradient of the polar angle $\theta$, has $Q_x = P_y$, and has circulation $2\pi$ once around the origin.
Having a potential function on a small disk around every point of the region, but not necessarily on the whole region. On a simply connected region, locally conservative fields are conservative.

The net number of counterclockwise turns a closed curve makes around a point (clockwise turns count as negative): $w = \frac{1}{2\pi}\oint_C\frac{-y\,dx + x\,dy}{x^2 + y^2}$ for the origin. Always an integer.

If $Q_x = P_y$ on the region between two simple closed curves, oriented the same way, then the field has the same circulation around both curves. It follows from Green's theorem for a region with a hole.

An idealized swirling flow with velocity field $\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\mathbf V$, where $\mathbf V$ is the vortex field: circulation $\Gamma$ around any loop that encloses it once, and zero curl everywhere else.

The area of a polygon with vertices $(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n)$ listed counterclockwise: $A = \tfrac12\sum(x_iy_{i+1} - x_{i+1}y_i)$, with $(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) = (x_1, y_1)$. It is Green's area formula applied edge by edge.

Area with a sign that records orientation: positive when the boundary runs counterclockwise, negative when it runs clockwise. The triangle $O$, $(x_a, y_a)$, $(x_b, y_b)$ has signed area $\tfrac12(x_ay_b - x_by_a)$.
Using the sign of a shoelace sum (or of $x_ay_b - x_by_a$ for a triangle) to tell whether points run counterclockwise (positive) or clockwise (negative).

A solid that is of type 1 (between two graphs over a region in the $xy$-plane) and also of the matching types for the $x$- and $y$-directions, such as a ball, a box or a cylinder. The Divergence theorem is first proved for these.

The statement $\int_{\partial M}\omega = \int_M d\omega$ about differential forms, of which the FTC, the fundamental theorem for line integrals, Green's, Stokes' and the Divergence theorem are all special cases.
On a surface with unit normal $\mathbf n$, the directional derivative $\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial n} = \nabla v\cdot\mathbf n$ of a function $v$ in the normal direction.

$\iiint_E\left(u\,
abla^2v + 
abla u\cdot
abla vight)dV = \iint_S u\,\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial n}\,dS$, from the Divergence theorem applied to $u
abla v$.

$\iiint_E\left(u\,\nabla^2v - v\,\nabla^2u\right)dV = \iint_S\left(u\,\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial n} - v\,\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial n}\right)dS$, the first identity minus its copy with $u$ and $v$ swapped.
The PDE $\nabla^2u = f$, where $f$ describes sources; with $f = 0$ it is Laplace's equation.
Solving $\nabla^2u = f$ in a region with the values of $u$ prescribed on the boundary. It has at most one solution.

Solving $\nabla^2u = f$ in a region with the normal derivative $\partial u/\partial n$ prescribed on the boundary. Solutions differ only by a constant, and exist only if $\iint_S\partial u/\partial n\,dS = \iiint_E f\,dV$.
Green's first identity with $u = v = w$: $\iiint_E|\nabla w|^2\,dV = \iint_S w\,\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial n}\,dS - \iiint_E w\,\nabla^2w\,dV$; used to prove uniqueness.
A function $f$ with $\mathbf F = \nabla f$ (physics often writes $\mathbf F = -\nabla\phi$ instead). The same thing as a potential function; the word "scalar" contrasts it with a vector potential.

A vector field $\mathbf A$ with $\nabla\times\mathbf A = \mathbf F$. Only divergence-free fields can have one; on all of space or a star-shaped region every one does. In magnetism, $\mathbf B = \nabla\times\mathbf A$.
Having divergence zero: $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F = 0$. Every curl is solenoidal; on all of space every solenoidal field is a curl.

Describes a region containing a point that can be joined to every other point of the region by a straight segment inside the region. Balls, boxes and all of space are star-shaped; space minus a point is not.
On a star-shaped region, a field with zero curl is a gradient and a field with zero divergence is a curl (stated here for vector fields in space; the general form is about differential forms).
Replacing a vector potential $\mathbf A$ by $\mathbf A + \nabla\chi$. It does not change $\nabla\times\mathbf A$, so a vector potential is never unique.

The choice of vector potential with $
abla\cdot\mathbf A = 0$, reached from any $\mathbf A$ by adding $
abla\chi$ with $
abla^2\chi = -
abla\cdot\mathbf A$.

Writing a vector field that dies off at infinity as $\mathbf F = -
abla\phi + 
abla	imes\mathbf A$, a curl-free part plus a divergence-free part; $
abla\cdot\mathbf F$ is the source of $\phi$ and $
abla	imes\mathbf F$ the source of $\mathbf A$.
For a Jacobian, the magnitude $|J|$ used as the area or volume scaling factor in a change of variables, since areas are positive even when a map reverses orientation.
The derivative of velocity, $\mathbf a(t) = \mathbf v'(t) = \mathbf r''(t)$; a vector.

For steady currents, the circulation of a magnetic field around a closed loop equals $\mu_0$ times the current through it: $\oint_C\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf r = \mu_0I_{\text{enc}}$. Maxwell's extra term handles changing electric fields.
The length of a curve, $L = \int_a^b|\mathbf r'(t)|\,dt$.
The distance along a curve from a starting time, $s(t) = \int_a^t|\mathbf r'(u)|\,du$, so $ds/dt = |\mathbf r'(t)|$.
The integral of a function divided by the size of the region: $f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{A(R)}\iint_R f\,dA$ (or divided by volume for a triple integral).
For a quadric surface, the coordinate axis along the odd-one-out variable (the linear variable of a paraboloid, or the one with the different sign in a cone or hyperboloid).
The unit vector $\mathbf B = \mathbf T\times\mathbf N$, perpendicular to the osculating plane of a curve.
A set in the plane or in space that fits inside some disk or ball.
The balance point of an object: $\bar x = M_y/m$, $\bar y = M_x/m$ (and $\bar z = M_{xy}/m$ in space).
The force directed toward the center that keeps an object in circular motion; magnitude $mv^2/R = mR\omega^2$.
The center of mass of a region of constant density; it depends only on the shape.
Rule for differentiating composites. In several variables: $\dfrac{dz}{dt} = f_x\dfrac{dx}{dt} + f_y\dfrac{dy}{dt}$, one term per path in the tree diagram.
The line integral $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$ of a field around a closed curve; it measures how much the field flows along the curve.
If $f_{xy}$ and $f_{yx}$ are continuous near a point, they are equal there.
A set that contains all of its boundary points, like a disk together with its circle.
A curve whose terminal point equals its initial point.
A surface that is the boundary of a solid region, such as a sphere or the surface of a cube; oriented outward by convention.
The scalar functions $P, Q, R$ in a vector field $\mathbf F = \langle P, Q, R\rangle$ (or $f, g, h$ in a vector function).
The entries $v_1, v_2, v_3$ of a vector $\langle v_1, v_2, v_3\rangle$.

The quadric surface $\dfrac{z^2}{c^2} = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2}$; horizontal traces are ellipses, vertical traces are hyperbolas, except in planes through the axis, where they are pairs of crossing lines.
A vector field that is the gradient of a scalar function, $\mathbf F = \nabla f$. Its line integrals are path independent.
The conservation-of-mass law $\partial\rho/\partial t + \nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf v) = 0$ for a fluid with density $\rho$ and velocity $\mathbf v$.
$f$ is continuous at $(a, b)$ if $\lim_{(x,y)\to(a,b)}f(x,y) = f(a, b)$.
A drawing of several level curves of a function, labeled with their values, usually equally spaced.
The $xy$-, $yz$- and $xz$-planes, which divide space into eight octants.
Lying in a common plane. Three vectors are coplanar exactly when their scalar triple product is 0.
A point where $\nabla f = \mathbf 0$ or a partial derivative does not exist; local extrema occur only at critical points.
The vector $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b$ perpendicular to both $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ (right-hand rule), with length $|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\sin\theta$.
$\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F = \nabla\times\mathbf F = \langle R_y - Q_z, P_z - R_x, Q_x - P_y\rangle$; it measures the rotation of a field.
How sharply a curve bends: $\kappa = |d\mathbf T/ds| = |\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''|/|\mathbf r'|^3$.
A surface made of all lines parallel to a given line through a plane curve; an equation missing one variable is a cylinder parallel to that variable's axis.
Coordinates $(r, \theta, z)$ with $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$; volume element $dV = r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$.
The limit of Riemann sums $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$; for $f \ge 0$, the area under the graph.

The operator $
abla = \langle\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_zangle$, used to write the gradient $
abla f$, divergence $
abla\cdot\mathbf F$ and curl $
abla	imes\mathbf F$.
Mass (or charge, population...) per unit area or volume; integrating it gives the total.
The instantaneous rate of change $f'(x) = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$, the slope of the graph.

$f(x, y)$ is differentiable at a point if its linear approximation is accurate in every direction: the error goes to zero faster than the distance to the point. Continuous partial derivatives guarantee it.
The quantity $dz = f_x\,dx + f_y\,dy$, the change along the tangent plane; it approximates the actual change $\Delta z$.
A physical law stated at points using derivatives (div, curl), such as $\nabla\cdot\mathbf E = \rho/\varepsilon_0$.
The angles a vector makes with the positive coordinate axes; their cosines are the components of its unit vector.
A vector parallel to a line, used in $\mathbf r = \mathbf r_0 + t\mathbf v$.
The rate of change of $f$ in the direction of a unit vector $\mathbf u$: $D_{\mathbf u}f = \nabla f\cdot\mathbf u$.
In the second-derivative test, $D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - (f_{xy})^2$ at a critical point.
$\operatorname{div}\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot\mathbf F = P_x + Q_y + R_z$; the net outflow per unit volume at a point.
For a closed surface $S$ bounding $E$, oriented outward: $\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S = \iiint_E\operatorname{div}\mathbf F\,dV$.
The set of inputs where a function is defined; for $f(x,y)$ it is a region in the plane.
The number $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3 = |\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta$.
The limit of double Riemann sums $\iint_R f\,dA$; for $f \ge 0$, the volume under the surface over $R$.
A sum $\sum\sum f(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)\,\Delta A$ over a grid of small rectangles.
The quadric surface $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$; all traces are ellipses.
The quadric surface $\dfrac zc = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2}$: a bowl with elliptical horizontal traces and parabolic vertical traces.
Extreme Value Theorem: a continuous function on a closed, bounded set attains an absolute maximum and minimum.
A curve $\mathbf r(t)$ that follows a vector field, $\mathbf r'(t) = \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))$; the path of a particle carried by the flow.
The surface integral $\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,dS$ measuring how much of a field passes through a surface (in 2D, $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds$ across a curve).
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: if $F' = f$ is continuous, $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$.
Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals: $\int_C\nabla f\cdot d\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a))$.
For continuous $f$ on a rectangle (or box), the double (or triple) integral equals the iterated integral in any order.
A rule assigning one number $f(x, y)$ to each point $(x, y)$ of a domain in the plane.
The electric flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by $\varepsilon_0$; in differential form $\nabla\cdot\mathbf E = \rho/\varepsilon_0$.
The vector of partial derivatives $\nabla f = \langle f_x, f_y, f_z\rangle$; it points in the direction of steepest increase and is perpendicular to level sets.
The vector field $\nabla f$ of a scalar function $f$.
For $f(x, y)$, the surface $z = f(x, y)$ in space.
For a positively oriented simple closed curve $C$ bounding $D$: $\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D(Q_x - P_y)\,dA$.
A curve on a parametric surface obtained by holding one parameter fixed.
A function whose Laplacian is zero, $\nabla^2 f = 0$.
The PDE $\partial T/\partial t = \alpha\nabla^2T$ governing heat conduction.
A space curve such as $\langle\cos t, \sin t, t\rangle$ that winds around a cylinder while rising steadily.
The matrix of second partial derivatives $\begin{bmatrix} f_{xx} & f_{xy}\\ f_{xy} & f_{yy}\end{bmatrix}$; its determinant is the discriminant $D$.
The saddle-shaped quadric $\dfrac zc = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2}$, with hyperbolic horizontal traces.
The connected quadric $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$ (one minus sign).
The quadric $-\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$ (two minus signs), made of two separate pieces.
If $F(x, y, z) = 0$ and $F_z \ne 0$ at a point, then near it the equation defines $z$ as a differentiable function of $x$ and $y$.
A fluid flow with zero divergence everywhere: no net outflow from any region.
A line integral is independent of path if all paths with the same endpoints give the same value; true exactly for conservative fields (on open connected regions).
A physical law stated about whole regions using flux or circulation integrals, such as Gauss's law $\iint_S\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf S = Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$.
The product rule backwards: $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$.
A vector field with zero curl.
An integral evaluated one variable at a time from the inside out, such as $\int_a^b\int_c^d f\,dy\,dx$.
The determinant $\dfrac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(u, v)} = x_uy_v - x_vy_u$; its absolute value is the area scaling factor of a transformation.
A function $f(x, y) \ge 0$ with $\iint_{\mathbb R^2}f\,dA = 1$ describing two continuous random variables; $P\big((X, Y)\in D\big) = \iint_D f\,dA$.
The energy of motion $K = \tfrac12m|\mathbf v|^2$.
The scalar $\lambda$ in $\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g$, the condition for an extremum of $f$ subject to $g = k$; it equals the rate of change of the optimal value with $k$.
A thin flat plate, modeled as a plane region with a density per unit area.
$\nabla^2 f = \operatorname{div}(\nabla f) = f_{xx} + f_{yy} + f_{zz}$.
The line $y = mx + b$ whose slope and intercept minimize the sum of squared residuals $\sum(y_i - mx_i - b)^2$ for data $(x_i, y_i)$; it passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$.
The set of points where $f(x, y) = c$ for a constant $c$.
The set of points where $f(x, y, z) = c$.
An integral along a curve: either $\int_C f\,ds$ (scalar) or $\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$ (vector), computed with a parametrization.
The approximation $f(x, y) \approx L(x, y)$ of a function by its linearization near a point.
$L(x, y) = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)(x - a) + f_y(a,b)(y - b)$, the function whose graph is the tangent plane.
A point where $f$ is at least as large as at all nearby points.
A point where $f$ is at most as large as at all nearby points.
The length of a vector, $|\mathbf v| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + v_3^2}$.
Total amount of matter; for a lamina $m = \iint_D\rho\,dA$, for a solid $m = \iiint_E\rho\,dV$.
For a projectile launched at speed $v_0$ and angle $\alpha$, $H = \dfrac{(v_0\sin\alpha)^2}{2g}$.
Fitting a model to data by choosing its coefficients to minimize the sum of the squared residuals, found by setting the partial derivatives of that sum to zero.
Mass weighted by distance from an axis (or plane), e.g. $M_y = \iint x\rho\,dA$; used to locate the center of mass.
Mass weighted by squared distance from an axis, e.g. $I_0 = \iint(x^2 + y^2)\rho\,dA$; resistance to rotational acceleration.
Force equals mass times acceleration, $\mathbf F = m\mathbf a$.
For acceleration, $a_N = \kappa v^2 = |\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''|/|\mathbf r'|$, the part that changes direction. For a field on a surface, $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n$.
The linear equations for the least squares line, from $S_m = 0$ and $S_b = 0$: $m\sum x_i^2 + b\sum x_i = \sum x_iy_i$ and $m\sum x_i + nb = \sum y_i$.
The line through a point of a surface in the direction of the normal vector, e.g. $\mathbf r_0 + t\nabla F(P)$.
A vector perpendicular to a plane or surface; for $ax + by + cz = d$ it is $\langle a, b, c\rangle$, for a parametric surface $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$.
A surface on which a unit normal can be chosen continuously everywhere (a Möbius strip is not orientable).
A choice of direction: of travel along a curve, or of unit normal on a surface. Reversing it flips the sign of vector line integrals and flux.
Perpendicular; two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is 0.
The circle that best fits a curve at a point, on its concave side, with radius $1/\kappa$.
The plane spanned by $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ at a point of a curve; its normal is $\mathbf B$.
Two nonzero vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other (equivalently, their cross product is $\mathbf 0$).
A slanted box with edges $\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf c$; its volume is $|\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)|$.
A curve given by coordinates as functions of a parameter, $x = x(t)$, $y = y(t)$.
Equations $x = x_0 + at$, $y = y_0 + bt$, $z = z_0 + ct$ giving each coordinate of a line (or curve) in terms of a parameter.
A surface given by $\mathbf r(u, v) = \langle x(u,v), y(u,v), z(u,v)\rangle$ for $(u, v)$ in a region $D$.
The derivative of $f$ with respect to one variable with the others held constant, e.g. $f_x = \partial f/\partial x$.
Partial differential equation: an equation relating an unknown function to its partial derivatives, such as the heat equation $u_t = u_{xx}$.
A mechanical instrument that measures the area of a region by tracing its boundary, an application of Green's theorem.
Coordinates $(r, \theta)$ with $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$; area element $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$.
A region $a \le r \le b$, $\alpha \le \theta \le \beta$: a sector of a ring.
The vector from the origin to a point; $\langle x, y, z\rangle$ for the point $(x, y, z)$.
For a closed curve bounding a region, counterclockwise (region on the left); for the boundary of a surface, the direction given by the right-hand rule.
A function $U$ with $\mathbf F = -\nabla U$ for a conservative force; the work done equals the loss of $U$.
A scalar function $f$ with $\nabla f = \mathbf F$.
The unit vector $\mathbf N = \mathbf T'/|\mathbf T'|$ pointing in the direction a curve is turning.
The shadow of a curve or solid on a coordinate plane, obtained by dropping a coordinate; for a solid, the region $D$ over which the outer integrals run.
The graph of a second-degree equation in $x, y, z$: ellipsoids, paraboloids, cones and hyperboloids.
A vector field pointing along the position vector (directly toward or away from the origin) at every point.
The reciprocal $\rho = 1/\kappa$ of the curvature: the radius of the osculating circle.
The set of output values of a function. (For a projectile, "range" also means the horizontal distance traveled, $v_0^2\sin2\alpha/g$ on level ground.)
Observed minus predicted value for a data point, $e_i = y_i - (mx_i + b)$: the vertical gap between the point and a fitted line.
The sum of several forces (or other vectors) acting together.
Curl the fingers of the right hand from the first direction to the second; the thumb gives the third (orientation of axes, $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b$, and boundary orientation in Stokes' theorem).
A critical point where $f$ takes both larger and smaller values arbitrarily close by; the second-derivative test gives $D < 0$.
A real number, as opposed to a vector.
The equation $ax + by + cz = d$ of a plane, whose coefficients give a normal vector.
The integral $\int_C f\,ds = \int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))|\mathbf r'(t)|\,dt$; independent of direction.
The signed length of the shadow of $\mathbf b$ on the line of $\mathbf a$: $\operatorname{comp}_{\mathbf a}\mathbf b = \dfrac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{|\mathbf a|}$.
The number $\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)$, a $3\times3$ determinant; its absolute value is the volume of a parallelepiped.
At a critical point with $D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2$: $D > 0, f_{xx} > 0$ min; $D > 0, f_{xx} < 0$ max; $D < 0$ saddle; $D = 0$ inconclusive.
Partial derivatives of partial derivatives: $f_{xx}, f_{xy}, f_{yx}, f_{yy}$.
A closed curve that does not cross itself.
A connected region in which every simple closed curve encloses only points of the region (no holes).
A point where a field has negative divergence: more flows in than out.
Lines in space that are not parallel and do not intersect.
Having continuous derivatives and a nonzero tangent or normal: for a parametric surface, $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v \ne \mathbf 0$.
A point where a field has positive divergence: more flows out than in.
The curve traced by the tip of a vector function $\mathbf r(t)$ in space.
The length of the velocity vector, $|\mathbf r'(t)| = ds/dt$.
All points at distance $r$ from a center $(h, k, l)$: $(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 + (z-l)^2 = r^2$.
Coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ with $x = \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta$, $y = \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta$, $z = \rho\cos\phi$; $dV = \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\theta\,d\phi$.
The unit vectors $\mathbf i = \langle 1,0,0\rangle$, $\mathbf j = \langle 0,1,0\rangle$, $\mathbf k = \langle 0,0,1\rangle$ along the axes.
For an oriented surface $S$ with boundary $C$ (right-hand rule): $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \iint_S\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S$.
The chain rule backwards: with $u = g(x)$, $\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx = \int f(u)\,du$ (change the limits too).
The total misfit of a model to data, $S = \sum e_i^2$, the sum of the squared residuals; least squares minimizes it.
$dS = |\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v|\,du\,dv$, the area of a small patch of a parametric surface.
Equations $\dfrac{x - x_0}{a} = \dfrac{y - y_0}{b} = \dfrac{z - z_0}{c}$ of a line, from solving the parametric equations for $t$.
Touching a curve and pointing along it; $\mathbf r'(t)$ is tangent to the curve $\mathbf r(t)$.
The plane that best approximates a surface at a point: $z = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)(x - a) + f_y(a,b)(y - b)$.

glossary.term: tangent plane to a level surface
glossary.definition: At $P$ on $F(x, y, z) = k$, the plane $\nabla F(P)\cdot\langle x - x_0, y - y_0, z - z_0\rangle = 0$.
The derivative $\mathbf r'(t)$, which points along the curve in the direction of motion.
The part of a vector along the direction of motion: $a_T = \dfrac{\mathbf r'\cdot\mathbf r''}{|\mathbf r'|}$ for acceleration, $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf T$ for a field along a curve.
The system of ordered triples $(x, y, z)$ on three mutually perpendicular axes oriented by the right-hand rule.
For a projectile over level ground, $t = \dfrac{2v_0\sin\alpha}{g}$.
The moving frame of unit tangent $\mathbf T$, principal normal $\mathbf N$ and binormal $\mathbf B$ along a curve.
The turning effect of a force: $\boldsymbol\tau = \mathbf r\times\mathbf F$.
The rate $\tau$ at which a curve twists out of its osculating plane, defined by $d\mathbf B/ds = -\tau\mathbf N$.
The curve in which a surface meets a plane, usually one parallel to a coordinate plane.
A map $T(u, v) = (x(u,v), y(u,v))$ from one plane to another, used for changes of variables.
A diagram of dependencies used with the chain rule: multiply derivatives along each path and add over paths.
The integral $\iiint_E f\,dV$ of a function over a solid region.
A solid lying between two surfaces $z = u_1(x, y)$ and $z = u_2(x, y)$ over a region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.
A plane region $a \le x \le b$, $g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)$ (between two graphs of $x$).
A plane region $c \le y \le d$, $h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)$ (between two graphs of $y$).
$\mathbf T(t) = \mathbf r'(t)/|\mathbf r'(t)|$.
A vector of length 1; $\mathbf v/|\mathbf v|$ is the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v$.
A quantity with length and direction, written $\langle v_1, v_2, v_3\rangle$.
The calculus of vector fields: line and surface integrals, curl, divergence, and the theorems of Green, Stokes and Gauss.
A function assigning a vector $\mathbf F(x, y) = \langle P, Q\rangle$ (or $\langle P, Q, R\rangle$ in space) to each point.
The integral $\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \int_a^b\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,dt$; it changes sign when the direction is reversed.
The vector $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf a}\mathbf b = \dfrac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{|\mathbf a|^2}\mathbf a$, the part of $\mathbf b$ along $\mathbf a$.
A function $\mathbf r(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t)\rangle$ that outputs a vector for each value of $t$.
The derivative of position, $\mathbf v(t) = \mathbf r'(t)$; a vector tangent to the path.
Force times displacement along the motion: $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf D$ for a constant force, $\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$ in general.
A sum of function values times small lengths, areas or volumes; its limit defines the integral.
A one-sided surface made by giving a strip a half twist before joining its ends; it is not orientable.
The four laws of electromagnetism (Gauss for $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$, Faraday, Ampère–Maxwell), in integral or differential form.
Heat flux is proportional to minus the temperature gradient: $\mathbf q = -k\nabla T$.
A changing magnetic flux induces circulation of the electric field: $\nabla\times\mathbf E = -\partial\mathbf B/\partial t$.

references.title: Differential calculus formulas
references.body:
## Single-variable review

| Rule | Formula |
|---|---|
| Chain rule | $\frac{d}{dx}f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))g'(x)$ |
| Product, quotient | $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$, $(f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g^2$ |
| FTC | $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$ where $F' = f$ |
| Parts | $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$ |
| Polar | $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$; area $\tfrac12\int r^2\,d\theta$ |

## Vector functions and motion

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Velocity, speed, acceleration | $\mathbf v = \mathbf r'$, $\lvert\mathbf r'\rvert$, $\mathbf a = \mathbf r''$ |
| Arc length | $L = \int_a^b\lvert\mathbf r'(t)\rvert\,dt$ |
| Unit tangent | $\mathbf T = \mathbf r'/\lvert\mathbf r'\rvert$ |
| Principal normal, binormal | $\mathbf N = \mathbf T'/\lvert\mathbf T'\rvert$, $\mathbf B = \mathbf T\times\mathbf N$ |
| Curvature | $\kappa = \dfrac{\lvert\mathbf T'\rvert}{\lvert\mathbf r'\rvert} = \dfrac{\lvert\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\rvert}{\lvert\mathbf r'\rvert^3}$; for $y = f(x)$: $\dfrac{\lvert f''\rvert}{(1 + f'^2)^{3/2}}$ |
| Acceleration components | $a_T = \dfrac{\mathbf r'\cdot\mathbf r''}{\lvert\mathbf r'\rvert}$, $a_N = \dfrac{\lvert\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\rvert}{\lvert\mathbf r'\rvert} = \kappa v^2$ |
| Projectile | $\mathbf r = \langle v_0t\cos\alpha,\; v_0t\sin\alpha - \tfrac12gt^2\rangle$ |
| Range, flight time, height | $\dfrac{v_0^2\sin2\alpha}{g}$, $\dfrac{2v_0\sin\alpha}{g}$, $\dfrac{(v_0\sin\alpha)^2}{2g}$ |

## Partial derivatives

| Idea | Formula |
|---|---|
| Tangent plane | $z = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)(x-a) + f_y(a,b)(y-b)$ |
| Differential | $dz = f_x\,dx + f_y\,dy$ |
| Chain rule | $\dfrac{dz}{dt} = f_x\dfrac{dx}{dt} + f_y\dfrac{dy}{dt}$; one term per tree path |
| Implicit | $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{F_x}{F_y}$; $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = -\dfrac{F_x}{F_z}$ |
| Gradient | $\nabla f = \langle f_x, f_y, f_z\rangle$ |
| Directional derivative | $D_{\mathbf u}f = \nabla f\cdot\mathbf u$ ($\lvert\mathbf u\rvert = 1$); max $\lvert\nabla f\rvert$ |
| Level surface tangent plane | $\nabla F(P)\cdot\langle x-x_0, y-y_0, z-z_0\rangle = 0$ |
| Clairaut | $f_{xy} = f_{yx}$ when both are continuous near the point |

## Optimization

| Tool | Statement |
|---|---|
| Critical point | $\nabla f = \mathbf 0$ or undefined |
| Second-derivative test | At a critical point with continuous second partials, $D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2$: $D>0, f_{xx}>0$ min; $D>0, f_{xx}<0$ max; $D<0$ saddle; $D=0$ inconclusive |
| Closed region | Compare interior critical values with boundary extremes (include corners) |
| Lagrange | $\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g$, $g = k$ (needs $\nabla g \ne \mathbf 0$); two constraints: $\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g + \mu\nabla h$ ($\nabla g$, $\nabla h$ not parallel) |
| Least squares line | Minimize $S(m,b) = \sum(y_i - mx_i - b)^2$; normal equations $m\sum x_i^2 + b\sum x_i = \sum x_iy_i$, $m\sum x_i + nb = \sum y_i$ |
| Least squares formulas | $m = \dfrac{n\sum x_iy_i - \sum x_i\sum y_i}{n\sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2}$, $b = \bar y - m\bar x$; through the origin: $k = \sum x_iy_i/\sum x_i^2$ |

references.title: Multiple integrals and coordinate systems
references.body:
## Setting up

| Region | Integral |
|---|---|
| Rectangle | $\int_a^b\int_c^d f\,dy\,dx$ (either order, Fubini) |
| Type I | $\int_a^b\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)}f\,dy\,dx$ |
| Type II | $\int_c^d\int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)}f\,dx\,dy$ |
| Type 1 solid | $\iint_D\int_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)}f\,dz\,dA$ |

Outer limits are constants; inner limits depend only on outer variables. To reverse the
order, sketch the region and slice the other way.

## Coordinate systems

| System | Conversion | Element |
|---|---|---|
| Polar | $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$ | $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$ |
| Cylindrical | $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, $z = z$ | $dV = r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$ |
| Spherical | $x = \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta$, $y = \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta$, $z = \rho\cos\phi$ | $dV = \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\theta\,d\phi$ |
| General | $x = x(u,v)$, $y = y(u,v)$ | $dA = \left\lvert\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right\rvert du\,dv$ |

Ranges: $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$, $0 \le \phi \le \pi$. Surfaces: $r = c$ cylinder, $z = r$ cone,
$\rho = c$ sphere, $\phi = c$ cone.

Jacobian: $\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} = x_uy_v - x_vy_u = 1\Big/\dfrac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}$.

## Applications

| Quantity | Lamina ($dA$) | Solid ($dV$) |
|---|---|---|
| Area / volume | $\iint_D 1\,dA$ | $\iiint_E 1\,dV$ |
| Mass | $\iint_D\rho\,dA$ | $\iiint_E\rho\,dV$ |
| Moments | $M_y = \iint x\rho$, $M_x = \iint y\rho$ | $M_{yz} = \iiint x\rho$, $M_{xz} = \iiint y\rho$, $M_{xy} = \iiint z\rho$ |
| Center of mass | $\bar x = M_y/m$, $\bar y = M_x/m$ | $\bar x = M_{yz}/m$, $\bar y = M_{xz}/m$, $\bar z = M_{xy}/m$ |
| Average value | $\frac{1}{A}\iint f\,dA$ | $\frac1V\iiint f\,dV$ |
| Moment of inertia | $I_0 = \iint(x^2+y^2)\rho\,dA$ | $I_z = \iiint(x^2+y^2)\rho\,dV$ |
| Surface area of $z = f(x,y)$ | $\iint_D\sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2}\,dA$ | |
| Probability (joint density $f$) | $P\big((X,Y)\in D\big) = \iint_D f\,dA$, $E(X) = \iint x f\,dA$ | |

## Useful values

| Integral | Value |
|---|---|
| $\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$ | $\pi$ |
| $\int_0^\pi\sin\phi\,d\phi$ | $2$ |
| $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx$ | $\sqrt\pi$ |
| Ball, radius $a$ | $V = \tfrac43\pi a^3$, surface $4\pi a^2$ |
| Tetrahedron $\frac xa + \frac yb + \frac zc \le 1$ | $V = abc/6$ |
| Half-disk centroid | $\bar y = 4a/(3\pi)$ |
| Solid hemisphere centroid | $\bar z = 3a/8$ |

references.title: Vector calculus and the big theorems
references.body:
## Operators

| Operator | Formula | Type |
|---|---|---|
| Gradient | $\nabla f = \langle f_x, f_y, f_z\rangle$ | vector |
| Divergence | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F = P_x + Q_y + R_z$ | scalar |
| Curl | $\nabla\times\mathbf F = \langle R_y - Q_z,\; P_z - R_x,\; Q_x - P_y\rangle$ | vector |
| Laplacian | $\nabla^2 f = f_{xx} + f_{yy} + f_{zz}$ | scalar |

Identities: $\nabla\times(\nabla f) = \mathbf 0$, $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf F) = 0$.

## Line and surface integrals

| Integral | Computation |
|---|---|
| $\int_C f\,ds$ | $\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\lvert\mathbf r'(t)\rvert\,dt$ |
| $\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$ | $\int_a^b\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,dt = \int_C P\,dx + Q\,dy + R\,dz$ |
| Surface area | $\iint_D\lvert\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\rvert\,dA$ |
| $\iint_S f\,dS$ | $\iint_D f(\mathbf r(u,v))\lvert\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\rvert\,dA$ |
| Flux $\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S$ | $\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,dA$ |
| Flux, graph $z = g$ upward | $\iint_D(-Pg_x - Qg_y + R)\,dA$ |

Standard parametrizations: sphere $\langle a\sin\phi\cos\theta, a\sin\phi\sin\theta, a\cos\phi\rangle$ with
$\lvert\mathbf r_\phi\times\mathbf r_\theta\rvert = a^2\sin\phi$; cylinder $\langle a\cos\theta, a\sin\theta, z\rangle$
with factor $a$; cone $\langle r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta, r\rangle$ with factor $r\sqrt2$.

## Conservative fields

For $\mathbf F$ with continuous first partials on an open, simply connected region, the following are equivalent:
$\mathbf F = \nabla f$; $\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$ is path independent; $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = 0$
for every closed $C$; $P_y = Q_x$ (2D) or $\nabla\times\mathbf F = \mathbf 0$ (3D).

Find $f$: integrate $P$ in $x$, add $g(y, z)$, match the other components.

## The fundamental theorems

| Theorem | Statement |
|---|---|
| FTC | $\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$ |
| Line integrals | $\int_C\nabla f\cdot d\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a))$ |
| Green (circulation) | $\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D(Q_x - P_y)\,dA$ |
| Green (flux) | $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds = \iint_D(P_x + Q_y)\,dA$ |
| Stokes | $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf S$ |
| Divergence (Gauss) | $\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S = \iiint_E\nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV$ |

Orientation: Green, counterclockwise; Stokes, right-hand rule (thumb along $\mathbf n$);
Divergence, outward normal on a closed surface. Area: $A = \tfrac12\oint_C x\,dy - y\,dx$.

## Physics

| Law | Integral form | Differential form |
|---|---|---|
| Gauss | $\iint_S\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf S = Q/\varepsilon_0$ | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf E = \rho/\varepsilon_0$ |
| No monopoles | $\iint_S\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf S = 0$ | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B = 0$ |
| Faraday | $\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf r = -\frac{d}{dt}\iint\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf S$ | $\nabla\times\mathbf E = -\partial_t\mathbf B$ |
| Ampère (steady) | $\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf r = \mu_0I$ | $\nabla\times\mathbf B = \mu_0\mathbf J$ |
| Continuity | $\frac{d}{dt}\iiint\rho\,dV = -\iint\rho\mathbf v\cdot d\mathbf S$ | $\partial_t\rho + \nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf v) = 0$ |
| Heat | $\mathbf q = -k\nabla T$ | $T_t = \alpha\nabla^2T$ |

references.title: Vectors, lines, planes and surfaces
references.body:
## Vectors

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Distance | $\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2 + (z_2-z_1)^2}$ |
| Sphere | $(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 + (z-l)^2 = r^2$ |
| Magnitude | $\lvert\mathbf v\rvert = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + v_3^2}$ |
| Unit vector | $\mathbf v/\lvert\mathbf v\rvert$ |
| Dot product | $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3 = \lvert\mathbf a\rvert\lvert\mathbf b\rvert\cos\theta$ |
| Angle | $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{\lvert\mathbf a\rvert\lvert\mathbf b\rvert}$ |
| Scalar projection | $\operatorname{comp}_{\mathbf a}\mathbf b = \dfrac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{\lvert\mathbf a\rvert}$ |
| Vector projection | $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf a}\mathbf b = \dfrac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{\lvert\mathbf a\rvert^2}\mathbf a$ |
| Cross product | $\langle a_2b_3 - a_3b_2,\; a_3b_1 - a_1b_3,\; a_1b_2 - a_2b_1\rangle$ |
| $\lvert\mathbf a\times\mathbf b\rvert$ | $\lvert\mathbf a\rvert\lvert\mathbf b\rvert\sin\theta$ = parallelogram area |
| Triangle area | $\tfrac12\lvert\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}\rvert$ |
| Triple product | $\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) = \det[\mathbf a; \mathbf b; \mathbf c]$; volume $= \lvert\cdot\rvert$ |
| Work (constant force) | $W = \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf D$ |
| Torque | $\boldsymbol\tau = \mathbf r\times\mathbf F$ |

Tests: orthogonal ⇔ $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b = 0$; parallel ⇔ $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b = \mathbf 0$; coplanar ⇔ triple product $= 0$.

## Lines and planes

| Object | Equation |
|---|---|
| Line | $\mathbf r = \mathbf r_0 + t\mathbf v$; $x = x_0 + at$, $y = y_0 + bt$, $z = z_0 + ct$ |
| Symmetric form | $\dfrac{x-x_0}{a} = \dfrac{y-y_0}{b} = \dfrac{z-z_0}{c}$ |
| Segment $\mathbf r_0 \to \mathbf r_1$ | $(1-t)\mathbf r_0 + t\mathbf r_1$, $0 \le t \le 1$ |
| Plane | $a(x-x_0) + b(y-y_0) + c(z-z_0) = 0$, normal $\langle a,b,c\rangle$ |
| Plane through $P, Q, R$ | normal $\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}$ |
| Line of two planes | direction $\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2$ |
| Point to plane $ax + by + cz = d$ | $D = \dfrac{\lvert ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 - d\rvert}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$ |

## Quadric surfaces

| Surface | Equation | Traces |
|---|---|---|
| Ellipsoid | $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} + \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$ | ellipses |
| Elliptic paraboloid | $\frac zc = \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2}$ | ellipses, parabolas |
| Hyperbolic paraboloid | $\frac zc = \frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2}$ | hyperbolas, parabolas |
| Cone | $\frac{z^2}{c^2} = \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2}$ | ellipses, hyperbolas (line pairs through the axis) |
| Hyperboloid, one sheet | $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$ | ellipses, hyperbolas |
| Hyperboloid, two sheets | $-\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} + \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$ | ellipses ($\lvert z\rvert > c$), hyperbolas |

A missing variable means a cylinder parallel to that axis.

drills.title: Product rule with an exponential
drills.prompt: Differentiate $f(x) = x^{n}e^{{k:coef}x}$.
drills.solution:
Product rule with $u = x^{n}$ and $v = e^{{k:coef}x}$: $u' = {n}x^{nm1}$ and, by the chain rule, $v' = {k:coef}e^{{k:coef}x}$.
So $f'(x) = u'v + uv' =$ **${n}x^{nm1}e^{{k:coef}x} {k:signedcoef}x^{n}e^{{k:coef}x}$**.

drills.title: Definite integral by substitution
drills.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{a} x\,(x^2 + {k})^{n}\,dx$. (Exact fraction or 2 decimals.)
drills.solution:
Let $u = x^2 + {k}$, so $du = 2x\,dx$. The limits become $u = {k}$ and $u = {top}$:
$\dfrac12\displaystyle\int_{{k}}^{{top}} u^{n}\,du = \dfrac{u^{{n1}}}{2\cdot {n1}}\Big|_{{k}}^{{top}} = \dfrac{{top}^{{n1}} - {k}^{{n1}}}{{den}} =$ **{ans}**.

drills.title: Distance between points in space
drills.prompt: Find the distance between $P({x1}, {y1}, {z1})$ and $Q({x2}, {y2}, {z2})$. (2 decimals.)
drills.solution:
Differences: $\Delta x = {dx}$, $\Delta y = {dy}$, $\Delta z = {dz}$.
$|PQ| = \sqrt{({dx})^2 + ({dy})^2 + ({dz})^2} = \sqrt{{s}} \approx$ **{dist:num2}**.

drills.title: Linear combination of vectors
drills.prompt: Let $\mathbf u = \langle {u1}, {u2}, {u3}\rangle$ and $\mathbf v = \langle {v1}, {v2}, {v3}\rangle$. Find ${p:coef}\mathbf u {q:signedcoef}\mathbf v$.
drills.solution:
Scale each vector, then add componentwise:
first ${p}({u1}) + ({q})({v1}) = {w1}$, second ${p}({u2}) + ({q})({v2}) = {w2}$, third ${p}({u3}) + ({q})({v3}) = {w3}$.
Result: **$\langle {w1}, {w2}, {w3}\rangle$**.

drills.title: Unit vector in a given direction
drills.prompt: Find the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v = \langle {v1}, {v2}, {v3}\rangle$. (Exact fractions.)
drills.solution:
$|\mathbf v| = \sqrt{({v1})^2 + ({v2})^2 + ({v3})^2} = {L}$. Divide each component by {L}:
**$\left\langle {e1:texfrac}, {e2:texfrac}, {e3:texfrac}\right\rangle$**.

drills.title: Angle between two vectors
drills.prompt: Find the angle between $\mathbf a = \langle {a1}, {a2}, {a3}\rangle$ and $\mathbf b = \langle {b1}, {b2}, {b3}\rangle$, in degrees (1 decimal).
drills.solution:
$\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b = {dot}$, $|\mathbf a| \approx {la:num4}$, $|\mathbf b| \approx {lb:num4}$.
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|} \approx {cs:num4}$, so $\theta \approx$ **{ang:num1}°**.

drills.title: Vector projection
drills.prompt: Find $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf a}\mathbf b$ for $\mathbf a = \langle {a1}, {a2}, {a3}\rangle$ and $\mathbf b = \langle {b1}, {b2}, {b3}\rangle$. (Exact fractions.)
drills.solution:
$\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b = {dot}$ and $|\mathbf a|^2 = {aa}$, so $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf a}\mathbf b = {f:texfrac}\,\mathbf a =$
**$\left\langle {p1:texfrac}, {p2:texfrac}, {p3:texfrac}\right\rangle$**.

drills.title: Compute a cross product
drills.prompt: Compute $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b$ for $\mathbf a = \langle {a1}, {a2}, {a3}\rangle$ and $\mathbf b = \langle {b1}, {b2}, {b3}\rangle$.

drills.title: Area of a triangle in space
drills.prompt: Find the area of the triangle with vertices $P({px}, {py}, {pz})$, $Q({qx}, {qy}, {qz})$, $R({rx}, {ry}, {rz})$. (2 decimals.)
drills.solution:
$\overrightarrow{PQ} = \langle {u1}, {u2}, {u3}\rangle$, $\overrightarrow{PR} = \langle {v1}, {v2}, {v3}\rangle$.
$\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR} = \langle {c1}, {c2}, {c3}\rangle$, and half its length is the area: $\tfrac12\sqrt{({c1})^2 + ({c2})^2 + ({c3})^2} \approx$ **{area:num2}**.

drills.title: Volume of a parallelepiped
drills.prompt: Find the volume of the parallelepiped with edges $\mathbf a = \langle {a1}, {a2}, {a3}\rangle$, $\mathbf b = \langle {b1}, {b2}, {b3}\rangle$, $\mathbf c = \langle {c1}, {c2}, {c3}\rangle$.
drills.solution:
$\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) = \begin{vmatrix} {a1} & {a2} & {a3}\\ {b1} & {b2} & {b3}\\ {c1} & {c2} & {c3}\end{vmatrix} = {det}$.
The volume is its absolute value: **{vol}**.

drills.title: Plane through three points
drills.prompt: Find the plane through $P({px}, {py}, {pz})$, $Q({qx}, {qy}, {qz})$, $R({rx}, {ry}, {rz})$. Use the normal $\mathbf n = \overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}$ and write the plane as $n_1x + n_2y + n_3z = d$.
drills.solution:
$\overrightarrow{PQ} = \langle {u1}, {u2}, {u3}\rangle$ and $\overrightarrow{PR} = \langle {v1}, {v2}, {v3}\rangle$, so $\mathbf n = \langle {n1}, {n2}, {n3}\rangle$.
Then $d = \mathbf n\cdot P = ({n1})({px}) + ({n2})({py}) + ({n3})({pz}) = {d}$.
The plane is **${n1:coef}x {n2:signedcoef}y {n3:signedcoef}z = {d}$**.

drills.title: Distance from a point to a plane
drills.prompt: Find the distance from $({x1}, {y1}, {z1})$ to the plane ${a:coef}x {b:signedcoef}y {c:signedcoef}z = {d}$. (2 decimals.)

drills.title: Center and radius of a sphere
drills.prompt: Find the center $(h, k, l)$ and radius $r$ of the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 {m1:signedcoef}x {m2:signedcoef}y {m3:signedcoef}z {cst:signed} = 0$.
drills.solution:
Complete the square in each variable: each center coordinate is minus half that variable's linear coefficient,
so $h = -\tfrac12({m1}) = {h}$, $k = -\tfrac12({m2}) = {k}$ and $l = -\tfrac12({m3}) = {l}$.
Then $(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 + (z - l)^2 = h^2 + k^2 + l^2 - ({cst}) = {r}^2$.
Center **$({h}, {k}, {l})$**, radius **{r}**.

drills.title: Derivative of a vector function
drills.prompt: Find $\mathbf r'(t)$ for $\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle {a}t^{n},\; e^{{b:coef}t},\; \sin({c}t)\right\rangle$. Enter each component as an expression in $t$.
drills.solution:
Differentiate each component separately.
$\dfrac{d}{dt}\left({a}t^{n}\right) = {an}t^{{nm1}}$; $\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{{b:coef}t} = {b:coef}e^{{b:coef}t}$ (chain rule); $\dfrac{d}{dt}\sin({c}t) = {c}\cos({c}t)$ (chain rule).
So $\mathbf r'(t) =$ **$\left\langle {an}t^{{nm1}},\; {b:coef}e^{{b:coef}t},\; {c}\cos({c}t)\right\rangle$**.

drills.title: Position from velocity
drills.prompt: A particle has velocity $\mathbf r'(t) = \langle {ta}t,\; {tb}t^2,\; {c}\rangle$ and starts at $\mathbf r(0) = \langle {x0}, {y0}, {z0}\rangle$. Find its position at $t = {tt}$.
drills.solution:
Integrate each component and add the starting position: $\mathbf r(t) = \langle {a:coef}t^2 {x0:signed},\; {b:coef}t^3 {y0:signed},\; {c:coef}t {z0:signed}\rangle$.
At $t = {tt}$: **$\langle {X}, {Y}, {Z}\rangle$**.

drills.title: Length of a helix
drills.prompt: Find the length of the helix $\mathbf r(t) = \langle {R:coef}\cos t,\; {R:coef}\sin t,\; {h:coef}t\rangle$ for $0 \le t \le {tmax}\pi$. (2 decimals.)
drills.solution:
$\mathbf r'(t) = \langle -{R:coef}\sin t,\; {R:coef}\cos t,\; {h}\rangle$, so $|\mathbf r'(t)| = \sqrt{{R}^2\sin^2t + {R}^2\cos^2t + {h}^2} = \sqrt{{R}^2 + {h}^2} \approx {sp:num4}$, a constant speed.
$L = \displaystyle\int_0^{{tmax}\pi}\sqrt{{R}^2 + {h}^2}\,dt = {tmax}\pi\sqrt{{R}^2 + {h}^2} \approx$ **{L:num2}**.

drills.title: Curvature of a parabola
drills.prompt: Find the curvature of $y = {a:coef}x^2 {b:signedcoef}x$ at $x = {x0}$. (2 decimals.)
drills.solution:
$f'(x) = {ta}x {b:signed}$ gives $f'({x0}) = {slope}$, and $f''(x) = {ta}$.
$\kappa = \dfrac{|f''|}{(1 + f'^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{|{ta}|}{(1 + ({slope})^2)^{3/2}} \approx$ **{kap:num2}**. (Radius of curvature $1/\kappa \approx {rho:num2}$.)

drills.title: Tangential and normal acceleration
drills.prompt: A particle moves along $\mathbf r(t) = \langle {a:coef}t,\; {b:coef}t^2,\; {c:coef}t\rangle$. Find the tangential and normal components of its acceleration at $t = {t0}$. (2 decimals.)
drills.solution:
$\mathbf r'({t0}) = \langle {a}, {v2}, {c}\rangle$ with length $\approx {sp:num4}$, and $\mathbf r''({t0}) = \langle 0, {tb}, 0\rangle$.
$a_T = \dfrac{\mathbf r'\cdot\mathbf r''}{|\mathbf r'|} = \dfrac{({v2})({tb})}{{sp:num4}} \approx$ **{aT:num2}**.
$\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'' = \langle {cr1}, 0, {cr3}\rangle$, so $a_N = \dfrac{|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''|}{|\mathbf r'|} \approx$ **{aN:num2}**.

drills.title: Projectile range, height and flight time
drills.prompt: A projectile is launched over level ground at {v0} m/s, {ang}° above the horizontal. With $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ and no air resistance, find its flight time, range and maximum height. (2 decimals.)
drills.solution:
Components: $v_0\cos\alpha \approx {vx:num2}$ m/s and $v_0\sin\alpha \approx {vy:num2}$ m/s.
Flight time $t = \dfrac{2v_0\sin\alpha}{g} \approx$ **{T:num2} s**.
Range $R = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin2\alpha}{g} = \dfrac{{v0}^2\sin {ang2}^\circ}{9.8} \approx$ **{R:num2} m**.
Max height $H = \dfrac{(v_0\sin\alpha)^2}{2g} \approx$ **{H:num2} m**.

drills.title: Velocity and speed
drills.prompt: A particle has position $\mathbf r(t) = \langle {p:coef}t^2,\; {q:coef}t,\; {s3:coef}t^3\rangle$. Find its velocity and speed at $t = {t0}$. (Speed to 2 decimals.)
drills.solution:
$\mathbf v(t) = \mathbf r'(t) = \langle {tp}t,\; {q},\; {ts}t^2\rangle$, so $\mathbf v({t0}) = \langle {vx}, {vy}, {vz}\rangle$.
Speed $= \sqrt{({vx})^2 + ({vy})^2 + ({vz})^2} \approx$ **{spd:num2}**.

drills.title: Evaluate a function of two variables
drills.prompt: Evaluate $f(x, y) = {a:coef}x^2y {b:signedcoef}y^2 - {c:coef}x$ at $({x0}, {y0})$.

drills.title: Read a level curve
drills.prompt: For $f(x, y) = {a:coef}x^2 + {b:coef}y^2$, find the value $c$ of the level curve through $({x0}, {y0})$, and where that level curve crosses the positive $x$-axis (2 decimals).
drills.solution:
$c = f({x0}, {y0}) = {a}({x0})^2 + {b}({y0})^2 =$ **{c}**. The level curve ${a:coef}x^2 + {b:coef}y^2 = {c}$ is an ellipse.
On the $x$-axis $y = 0$, so $x^2 = {c}/{a}$ and $x = \sqrt{{c}/{a}} \approx$ **{sx:num2}**.

drills.title: Limit along a line
drills.prompt: Find the limit of $f(x, y) = \dfrac{{a:coef}x^2 {b:signedcoef}y^2}{x^2 + y^2}$ as $(x, y)\to(0, 0)$ along the line $y = {m:coef}x$. (Exact fraction.)
drills.solution:
Substitute $y = {m:coef}x$: $\dfrac{{a:coef}x^2 + ({b})({m2})x^2}{(1 + {m2})x^2} = \dfrac{{num}}{{den}}$ for $x \ne 0$, so the limit along this line is **${L:texfrac}$**.
Because the answer depends on the slope (it is ${a}$ along the $x$-axis and ${b}$ along the $y$-axis), the two-variable limit does not exist.

drills.title: First partial derivatives
drills.prompt: Find $f_x$ and $f_y$ for $f(x, y) = {a}x^{m}y^{n} {b:signedcoef}xy$.
drills.solution:
For $f_x$, treat $y$ as a constant: $\partial_x\left({a}x^{m}y^{n}\right) = {am}x^{{m1}}y^{n}$ and $\partial_x({b:coef}xy) = {b:coef}y$.
For $f_y$, treat $x$ as a constant: $\partial_y\left({a}x^{m}y^{n}\right) = {an}x^{m}y^{{n1}}$ and $\partial_y({b:coef}xy) = {b:coef}x$.
**$f_x = {am}x^{{m1}}y^{n} {b:signedcoef}y$, $f_y = {an}x^{m}y^{{n1}} {b:signedcoef}x$.**

drills.title: Second partial derivatives
drills.prompt: For $f(x, y) = {a:coef}x^3y^2 {b:signedcoef}xy^3$, find $f_{xx}$, $f_{xy}$ and $f_{yy}$.
drills.solution:
First partials: $f_x = {a3}x^2y^2 {b:signedcoef}y^3$ and $f_y = {a2}x^3y {b3:signedcoef}xy^2$.
Then $f_{xx} = {a6}xy^2$, $f_{xy} = \partial_y f_x = {a6}x^2y {b3:signedcoef}y^2$ (and $f_{yx} = \partial_x f_y$ gives the same, by Clairaut), and $f_{yy} = {a2}x^3 {b6:signedcoef}xy$.
**$f_{xx} = {a6}xy^2$, $f_{xy} = {a6}x^2y {b3:signedcoef}y^2$, $f_{yy} = {a2}x^3 {b6:signedcoef}xy$.**

drills.title: Tangent plane to a graph
drills.prompt: Find the tangent plane to $z = {a:coef}x^2 {b:signedcoef}y^2 {c:signedcoef}xy$ at the point where $x = {x0}$, $y = {y0}$. Write it as $z = Ax + By + C$.

drills.title: Estimate with a linearization
drills.prompt: Use the linearization of $f(x, y) = {a:coef}x^2y$ at $({x0}, {y0})$ to estimate $f({x1}, {y1})$.
drills.solution:
$f({x0}, {y0}) = {f0}$, $f_x = 2({a})xy = {fx}$, $f_y = {a:coef}x^2 = {fy}$ at the base point.
$L = {f0} + {fx}({dx}) + {fy}({dy}) =$ **{Lv:num2}**. (The exact value is about {actual:num4}.)

drills.title: Chain rule along a path
drills.prompt: Let $z = x^2 {a:signedcoef}xy$ with $x = t^2 {b:signed}$ and $y = {c:coef}t$. Use the chain rule to find $\dfrac{dz}{dt}$ at $t = {t0}$.
drills.solution:
At $t = {t0}$: $x = {X}$, $y = {Y}$.
$z_x = 2x + ({a})y = {zx}$, $z_y = ({a})x = {zy}$, $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2t = {xt}$, $\dfrac{dy}{dt} = {yt}$.
$\dfrac{dz}{dt} = z_x\dfrac{dx}{dt} + z_y\dfrac{dy}{dt} = ({zx})({xt}) + ({zy})({yt}) =$ **{rate}**.

drills.title: Implicit differentiation
drills.prompt: The curve $x^2 {a:signedcoef}xy + y^3 = {k}$ passes through $({x0}, {y0})$. Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ there. (Exact fraction.)
drills.solution:
With $F = x^2 + ({a})xy + y^3 - ({k})$: $F_x = 2x + ({a})y = {Fx}$ and $F_y = ({a})x + 3y^2 = {Fy}$ at the point.
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{F_x}{F_y} = -\dfrac{{Fx}}{{Fy}} =$ **${slope:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Gradient of a function of three variables
drills.prompt: Find $\nabla f$ for $f(x, y, z) = {a:coef}x^2y {b:signedcoef}yz^2 {c:signedcoef}xz$.
drills.solution:
